items.title: Competing cognitive pathways associated with generative AI tool use and self-reported critical thinking in higher education
items.abstract: Background The increasing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has raised concerns about its relationship with students’ critical thinking, yet empirical findings remain inconsistent. Drawing on Social Cognitive Theory and Cognitive Offloading Theory, this study examined the competing indirect associations between GenAI tool use and self-reported critical thinking through self-regulated learning and cognitive offloading. It also investigated the sequential indirect association involving both mediators to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the cognitive-regulatory processes associated with GenAI-supported learning. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 378 undergraduate students from 10 universities in Jiangsu Province of China. Data were analyzed using covariance-based structural equation modeling (CB-SEM). Bias-corrected bootstrap analysis with 5,000 resamples was performed to examine direct, indirect, and total associations, as well as to compare the magnitudes of the competing indirect pathways. Results GenAI tool use was positively associated with self-regulated learning (β = 0.431, p < 0.001) and cognitive offloading (β = 0.390, p < 0.001). Self-regulated learning was positively associated with critical thinking (β = 0.368, p < 0.001), whereas cognitive offloading was negatively associated with critical thinking (β = −0.409, p < 0.001). Self-regulated learning was also negatively associated with cognitive offloading (β = −0.318, p < 0.001). The direct association between GenAI tool use and critical thinking was not statistically significant (β = −0.059, p = 0.316). Bootstrap analysis identified a positive indirect association through self-regulated learning (B = 0.147, 95% CI [0.096, 0.212]), a negative indirect association through cognitive offloading (B = −0.148, 95% CI [−0.219, −0.092]), and a positive sequential indirect association through self-regulated learning and cognitive offloading (B = 0.052, 95% CI [0.030, 0.088]). The total association was not statistically significant, and the two single-mediator indirect associations did not differ significantly in magnitude. Conclusion The relationship between GenAI tool use and critical thinking may be more complex than a uniformly beneficial or detrimental association. The findings reveal the coexistence of positive and negative indirect associations involving self-regulatory processes and cognitive offloading, highlighting the relevance of self-regulated learning in understanding how students engage with GenAI-supported learning. These results underscore the importance of supporting students’ self-regulatory capacities while encouraging thoughtful engagement with AI-generated information. Given the cross-sectional design and self-reported measures, the findings should be interpreted as statistical associations rather than causal effects. Longitudinal and experimental studies are needed to clarify the temporal relationships among these constructs and their implications for critical thinking development.

items.title: Deception Graphs Against Attacking AI Agents: A Concept Note
items.abstract: Public summary of a defensive research concept. Threat reports from 2026 describe a shift towards autonomous, multi-agent AI attack operations. This note proposes a "deception graph": the defender deliberately shapes what an attacking agent discovers, using model-guided trap placement on an attack graph, distinguishing agents from humans by the rhythm of their actions, fast automated containment within strict limits, and an autonomous maintenance loop. It summarizes simulation results on synthetic networks (over half a million attack runs) and sets out principles for autonomous defense, ethical boundaries (no hack-back) and recommendations for organizations. Operational details are deliberately omitted; the full technical version has been shared with cybersecurity agencies under TLP:AMBER. Developed in collaboration with Claude (Anthropic) as an AI research assistant; see the disclosure in the paper.

items.title: Distributed Creativity: Rethinking Authorship in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in art and cultural production, reviving the question of who creates a work and to whom it should be attributed. This article situates AI-assisted production within a longer history of challenges to the figure of the solitary author, from Roland Barthes’s “death of the author” and Michel Foucault’s author function to the participatory practices of digital culture. It argues, however, that the distribution of authorship does not by itself demonstrate the distribution of creativity. Drawing on accounts that define creativity through novelty, value and social recognition, the article treats authorship, creativity and agency as related but analytically distinct questions. It then distinguishes two ideal types of distributed creativity: intentional-participatory distribution, in which contributors knowingly exercise some creative control over a shared work, as in The Johnny Cash Project and This Exquisite Forest; and infrastructural asymmetric distribution, in which people, labour or cultural materials enter a production system without comparable awareness or influence over the outcome, as exposed by Aaron Koblin’s The Sheep Market. Applied to generative AI, the distinction shows that users may work with models intentionally and iteratively while depending on training data, annotation work and infrastructures that remain largely invisible. Rather than treating AI as either an autonomous artist or a neutral tool, the article describes human– AI production systems in which creative control, attribution and benefit are unequally distributed, and it argues that questions of credit, consent and fair compensation must be addressed alongside, but separately from, the question of authorship.

items.title: Effects of generative AI on self-regulated learning and the incremental contributions of instructional interventions: evidence from a meta-analysis
items.abstract: Introduction Self-regulated learning (SRL) is a core competency essential to students' autonomous learning and their sustainable development. Generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) offers new possibilities for supporting SRL. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of Gen-AI and the added value of accompanying instructional interventions remain insufficiently explored. Methods This meta-analysis synthesizes 26 independent studies published between 2023 and 2026, contributing 76 effect sizes, and employs a three-level random-effects model to examine two separate comparative frameworks. Of the included studies, 18 compared Gen-AI-supported learning with learning without AI, while 10 compared Gen-AI combined with instructional interventions with Gen-AI used alone. Two studies provided effect sizes for both types of comparisons. Results In the first framework, we separately compared standalone Gen-AI and Gen-AI combined with instructional interventions with the no-AI learning condition, examining their overall effects on SRL. Standalone Gen-AI produces a statistically significant moderate positive effect on students' SRL (ḡ = 0.508, 95% CI [0.261, 0.755]), whereas Gen-AI combined with structured instructional interventions produces a statistically significant moderate positive effect (ḡ= 0.788, 95% CI [0.579, 0.996]). Although the latter yields a larger estimated effect, the difference between the two estimated effects was not statistically significant (Q between = 2.887, df = 1, p = 0.089). These findings suggest that both standalone Gen-AI and Gen-AI combined with instructional interventions can improve students' SRL relative to learning without AI, but do not establish that combining Gen-AI with instructional interventions is significantly more effective than using Gen-AI alone. In the second framework, we directly compared Gen-AI combined with instructional interventions against Gen-AI alone to examine the incremental contribution of instructional interventions when Gen-AI is already being used. The results revealed a statistically significant moderate positive incremental effect of instructional interventions (ḡ= 0.528, 95% CI [0.359, 0.697]), indicating that instructional interventions provided additional benefits for students' SRL beyond those associated with Gen-AI use alone. Discussion Overall, this study distinguishes between the overall effects of Gen-AI-supported learning relative to no-AI conditions and the incremental contribution of instructional interventions when Gen-AI is already being used. These findings provide empirical evidence for educators, instructional designers, and future research.

items.title: ELSA in the field: studying ethical, legal, societal, and technological aspects of artificial intelligence in practice
items.abstract: In this article, we discuss ‘ELSA in the Field’, building on ELSA, i.e. taking into account various Ethical, Legal, and Societal Aspects of AI systems during development and deployment, and on Responsible Innovation (RI), i.e. a framework for addressing ethical and social concerns, through anticipation, reflexivity, inclusion, and responsiveness. The ‘ELSA in the Field’ approach involves a combination of desk research and field research, and aims to facilitate collaboration between ELSA/RI experts and relevant stakeholders to learn from their expertise, understand their contexts and practices, and identify their concerns, ambitions and questions. Critically, the fieldwork is focused on specific practices , involving the deployment of diverse technologies, e.g., of AI systems. The ethical, legal, societal, and technological aspects related to these specific practices are studied, so that technological aspects are on equal footing with ethical, legal, and societal aspects. This facilitates collaboration between ELSA/RI experts and technology-oriented people. The ‘ELSA in the Field’ is introduced and positioned relative to ELSA and RI. It is then described in practical terms and with examples from a research and innovation project in which the authors collaborate. The article closes with a discussion of participation, iteration, reflexivity, and boundary objects.

items.title: EMPOWERING EDUCATORS: USING THE C.O.D.E.S. FRAMEWORK TO DESIGN GENERATIVE AI USE STATEMENTS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has unsettled post-secondary assessment by raising questions about authorship, independent learner work, and assessment validity. Institutional policies and syllabus statements give general direction but seldom say how GenAI may be used in a particular assessment. This conceptual design paper introduces C.O.D.E.S., a framework written primarily for post-secondary instructors. Its five components ask instructors to Clarify the permitted level of GenAI use, offer instructional supports, define tools and purposes, Explain the rationale, and Set transparency and accountability expectations. The framework draws on backward design, adult learning principles, Transparency in Learning and Teaching, Universal Design for Learning, and reflective technology integration. It treats GenAI use statements as instructional design tools instead of compliance notices. Four use levels (Closed, Restricted, Conditional, and Open) place cognitive responsibility in different parts of the task. For example, a business instructor might allow GenAI to draft a crisis statement and then assess the learner’s verification, critique, revision, and professional justification. C.O.D.E.S. may help instructors align GenAI expectations with learning outcomes, privacy safeguards, equitable alternatives, and defensible evidence of learner capability. The framework is conceptual and still needs empirical evaluation across disciplines, assessment types, institutions, and learner populations.

items.title: Enterprise Safety Management in Healthcare: A Baldrige-Aligned Framework for Integrated Risk Governance
items.abstract: Healthcare safety is frequently managed through separate programs for patient harm, workforce injury, employee health, security, and organizational risk, although these domains share hazards, work systems, and governance dependencies. This conceptual article proposes an Enterprise Safety Management System (ESMS) comprising four interdependent management functions: Integrated Safety Systems, Leadership and Governance, Learning and Capability Systems, and Culture and Workforce Support. The preliminary architecture was derived from safety-management experience in high-risk industries and healthcare systems-engineering, integrated worker-safety, high-reliability, resilience, and safety-culture traditions. It was subsequently mapped to the revised July 2026 Baldrige Excellence Framework for Business, Nonprofit, and Government. The mapping examines the framework’s six categories, embedded category-level results, three maturity pathways, Approach–Deployment–Learning–Integration and Levels–Trends–Comparisons–Integration evaluation logic, Organizational Intelligence, and emphasis on agility, resilience, and artificial intelligence. Workplace violence prevention illustrates cross-domain reporting, governance, operational control, learning, workforce participation, support, and recovery. The ESMS and its Baldrige mapping are conceptual proposals, not validated constructs or interventions. Their principal implication is that healthcare organizations can examine safety as an integrated management system while preserving specialized expertise and regulatory responsibilities.

items.title: Evaluating Visual Encodings in Squarified Treemaps: Toward Effective Website Structure Navigation
items.abstract: Fact-finding tasks require users to locate specific information within website structures. This study examined how visual encoding in a squarified treemap affects user performance during such tasks. Two encodings, height and saturation, were used to represent structural metrics: the number of pages and the number of outgoing links. Using a between-participants design, users selected the region expected to lead to a target page. Regions represented groups of pages sharing the same directory path, e.g., /admissions or/research. Task completion time and error rate were recorded. Two baselines were included: without encoding and using real website navigation. Analysis showed that saturation encoding led to faster task completion and lower error rates, particularly when encoding outgoing links. Participants in the outgoing links with saturation condition completed tasks fastest and had the lowest error rate, while real-website navigation had the highest error rate. The findings demonstrate how appropriate encoding can improve performance in fact-finding tasks.

items.title: Evidence-Based Enhancement Plan to Optimize Technology Integration for Improved Teachers’ Instructional Productivity and Learners’ Engagement
items.abstract: This study examined the relationship between technology integration, teachers’ instructional productivity, and learners’ engagement in selected public elementary schools in Zone 2, Guindulman District, Schools Division of Bohol, Philippines, during School Year 2026–2027. Using a descriptive-correlational research design, data were collected from 178 respondents comprising three school heads, 35 teachers, and 140 learners through adapted and modified questionnaires. Data were analyzed using frequency, percentage, weighted mean, and Spearman’s rank-order correlation. Results revealed that technology integration was highly integrated (M = 3.70), teachers’ instructional productivity was highly productive (M = 3.72), and learners’ engagement was highly engaged (M = 3.55). Technology integration demonstrated significant positive relationships with teachers’ instructional productivity (ρ = 0.635, p < .001) and learners’ engagement (ρ = 0.490, p = .003). The study concludes that purposeful technology integration is associated with greater instructional productivity and learner engagement. Accordingly, implementing an evidence-based enhancement plan that prioritizes teachers’ technological competence and confidence, differentiated and personalized instruction, and cognitive engagement is recommended. The study’s localized setting, questionnaire-based assessments, and correlational design limit its generalizability and causal interpretation. Nevertheless, the findings provide empirical evidence for strengthening technology-supported instructional practices, professional development, and school-level decision-making. The study advances Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) and contributes to educational, technological, and institutional sustainability through responsible digital resource utilization, continuous teacher development, and meaningful learner engagement.

items.title: Evolving role of educators in higher education: an interview study on three perspectives
items.abstract: Existing research on AI in higher education has emphasized digital competencies and technology integration, however, less attention has been paid to how changing educator roles are understood across stakeholder groups and shaped by institutional conditions. This qualitative study examines how educators, students, and educational developers construct the evolving role of educators in response to educational technologies, including generative AI, and how these changes are shaped by emotional responses and institutional conditions. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 20 participants, the study employs inductive reflexive thematic analysis within a contextualist, interpretive framework, using interactionist role theory and, to a lesser extent, control-value theory to interpret role changes and emotional responses to technology, respectively. The findings indicate that the educator role is being renegotiated rather than replaced. Technology was predominantly framed as assistance rather than substitution, while educators remained positioned as responsible for pedagogical judgment, ethical oversight, and human guidance. Emotional responses to technology were mixed and often shaped by uncertainty, trust, and perceived control. Role adaptation was also described as strongly mediated by institutional conditions, including workload, large classes, research–teaching tensions, and uneven engagement with professional development. The paper contributes by shifting attention from technology adoption alone to the interactional, emotional, and institutional processes through which the educator’s role is being reworked in higher education.

items.title: Faculty psychological readiness for responsible AI integration in higher education: perceived policy support, teaching engagement, teaching innovation, and professional practice
items.abstract: Introduction Universities are developing policies for artificial intelligence (AI), but less is known about how faculty members' perceptions of policy support relate to their readiness and reported teaching practices. Methods This study examined psychological readiness for responsible AI integration (PRRAI) as a second-order construct with cognitive, affective, and ethical dimensions. We tested its indirect role in the associations between perceived policy support (PPS) and teaching engagement, teaching innovation behavior, and responsible AI professional practice. A cross-sectional survey conducted from June to August 2025 yielded 374 eligible responses from faculty members at 18 higher education institutions in Jiangsu Province, China. Results Structural equation modeling identified positive associations between PPS and PRRAI and between PRRAI and all three outcomes. The PPS-PRRAI coefficient was moderate (β = 0.52); a 1-SD increase in PPS corresponded to approximately 0.35 points on the five-point PRRAI scale. Indirect effects were significant for each outcome. After accounting for PRRAI, the direct association with PPS remained significant for responsible practice but not for engagement or innovation. AI literacy strengthened the PPS-PRRAI association, whereas teaching experience weakened the PRRAI-innovation association. Sensitivity analyses by primary AI referent and institution-clustered standard errors produced the same substantive pattern. Discussion Because the data are cross-sectional and self-reported, the findings concern perceived support and statistical associations rather than effects of actual policies or interventions.
